chapter_title: Objectives, Uses, and Products of Site Characterization Investigations

sections.title: General Objectives for Site Characterization
sections.summary: Investigations address one or more of eight objectives: stratigraphy, groundwater, design parameters, constructability, hazard identification, suitability, condition assessment and performance monitoring, and location and alignment. A hazard can harm a project; risk combines its likelihood and consequences.
sections.body: An "investigation" is a systematic study to identify ground conditions and characterize soil and rock behavior: subsurface (boring, probing, excavation, testing), geophysical, laboratory, and examination of maps and imagery; objectives and anticipated products should be understood first. Objectives: (1) Stratigraphy, discrete strata and cross-sections; (2) Groundwater Conditions (p. 2-2); (3) Design Parameters, reliable estimates; (4) Constructability; (5) Hazard Identification; (6) Suitability, e.g., engineered fill or aggregate source; (7) Condition Assessment and Performance Monitoring; (8) Location and Alignment. A "hazard" is a condition or feature with potential to negatively impact construction or operation; "risk" is potential loss, combining likelihood of the hazard affecting a project with consequences (costs). Suitability of tests depends on the objective: tests suited to hazard identification or alignment may suit design parameters poorly, and vice versa. Products serve different users (p. 2-3): designers use boring logs quantitatively for design models, planners qualitatively for cost estimates, bidders for construction methods and risks, and logs may become contract documents affecting bid prices and payment quantities. (pp. 2-1 to 2-3)
key_points: Eight objectives for investigations (pp. 2-1 to 2-2).
Hazard = potential to impact; risk = likelihood x consequence (p. 2-2).
Test suitability depends on the objective (p. 2-2).
Boring logs serve designers, planners, bidders and contracts differently (p. 2-3).
sections.applicability: Framework for identifying objectives before planning site characterization investigations

sections.title: Classes of Site Characterization investigations
sections.summary: Different classes or phases of investigations give a systematic approach to site characterization; terminology varies by organization, but the classes share common characteristics and objectives (2.2.1 to 2.2.7).
sections.body: Because objectives vary and may compete, different classes or phases of investigation are conducted for a systematic approach; terminology varies between organizations, but the classes share common characteristics and objectives, described in sections 2.2.1 to 2.2.7. (p. 2-3)
sections.applicability: Classification and scope planning for different investigation phases

sections.title: Desk Studies
sections.summary: Desk studies gather and evaluate available information before field work: prior investigations, performance records, geologic reports, maps, imagery, colleagues and regulations. They inform scoping, crew preparation, location and alignment, and early hazard identification.
sections.body: A critical first step for practically all programs is a desk study of available information, often completed before field or laboratory work. Sources: historical records of prior investigations at or near the site; performance records of nearby structures (even the popular press); geologic reports; geologic, soil survey, topographic, utility and insurance maps; aerial photographs, satellite imagery and other remote sensing; colleagues with local experience (p. 2-4); and pertinent laws, policies and regulations (e.g., U.S. Army Corps of Engineers rules, railroad and water quality regulations). Desk studies inform planning and scoping, help equip field crews for likely conditions, contribute to location and alignment decisions and to early identification of hazards (see section 3.2). (pp. 2-3 to 2-4)
key_points: Desk study is the first step for practically all programs (p. 2-3).
Sources: prior records, maps, imagery, colleagues, regulations (pp. 2-3 to 2-4).
Informs scoping, alignment and early hazard identification (p. 2-4).

sections.title: Preliminary Investigations
sections.summary: Preliminary investigations support planning and preliminary design with sparse shallow borings, test pits or soundings at wide spacing, disturbed samples for index tests, and scanning geophysics (seismic, MASW, resistivity) between borings; seldom high-quality samples.
sections.body: Preliminary investigations are performed early to support planning, give simple and often qualitative information for preliminary design, plan more rigorous investigations, and identify potential hazard risks. For roadways they often include relatively sparse shallow borings, test pits and/or in situ soundings at relatively large spacing along the alignment, with bulk or disturbed samples for "index property" tests; they seldom include higher quality samples for "performance" tests of strength and stress-strain properties. Scanning geophysical methods covering large areas (seismic reflection/refraction, MASW, electrical resistivity) help interpret conditions between sparse borings or soundings. (p. 2-4)
key_points: Sparse, shallow, widely spaced explorations (p. 2-4).
Disturbed samples for index tests; seldom high-quality samples (p. 2-4).
Scanning geophysics between borings (p. 2-4).

sections.title: Design Investigations
sections.summary: Design investigations follow alignment, grade and structure locations: more rigorous, targeted and costly, to confirm stratigraphy and establish reliable design parameters; large projects may have several phases, and special investigations address particular challenges.
sections.body: Design investigations are typically performed after alignment, grade and locations of walls, piers, abutments and cut/fill slopes are set; they are more rigorous, "targeted" and costly than preliminary investigations. Principal objectives (p. 2-5): (1) confirm or refine preliminary stratigraphy; (2) establish reliable values for design parameters; they may also address hazards and constructability. Large projects may have several phases; small projects may combine preliminary and design investigations, which introduces some risk. They use advanced boring, sampling, laboratory and in situ testing and possibly geophysics. "Special" investigations address specific challenges with uncommon tests or greater quantities, e.g., significant embankments on soft foundations, large or challenging bridges, karst, underground mines, seismic hazards or problematic geomaterials. (pp. 2-4 to 2-5)
key_points: Confirm stratigraphy and establish reliable design parameters (p. 2-5).
Combining with preliminary investigation introduces risk (p. 2-5).
Special investigations for specific challenges (p. 2-5).

sections.title: Borrow Site Investigations
sections.summary: Borrow site investigations characterize stratigraphy and soil or rock type (not in situ properties, which change on placement) with rapid borings, disturbed samples, index tests and test pits, then compacted specimen tests; similar investigations locate waste sites.
sections.body: Where substantial off-site borrow is needed, borrow site investigations evaluate potential sources, focusing on stratigraphy and general soil or rock type rather than in situ properties, which change with excavation, transport and placement (p. 2-6). They commonly use rapid, cost-effective borings, disturbed sampling and inexpensive index tests, plus test pits for large disturbed samples; as a source is confirmed, compacted specimens may be tested for engineering properties. Similar investigations identify locations for "wasting" unsuitable materials without harming the project, neighbors or environment (e.g., pyritic rock). (pp. 2-5 to 2-6)
key_points: Stratigraphy and material type, not in situ properties (p. 2-5).
Rapid borings, disturbed samples, index tests, test pits (p. 2-6).
Similar investigations for waste sites (p. 2-6).

sections.title: Investigations for Performance Monitoring and Condition Assessment
sections.summary: Performance monitoring and condition assessment investigations, during or after construction, often install instruments for stress, deformation, pore pressure or load (settlement plates, piezometers, inclinometers); practice is changing with asset management and is not addressed further.
sections.body: Investigations during or after construction characterize performance of features (walls, bridges, embankments) or support condition assessment, often installing instrumentation for stress, deformation, pore water pressure and/or load. Practice is changing substantially with asset management. They may guide construction (settlement plates and piezometers beneath embankments on soft soils) or follow problematic performance years later (inclinometers for slope or foundation movement). Because they document performance rather than characterize sites they are not addressed further (p. 2-7), though the manual's practices apply. (pp. 2-6 to 2-7)
key_points: Instrumentation for stress, deformation, pore pressure, load (p. 2-6).
Changing with asset management (p. 2-6).
Not addressed further in the manual (pp. 2-6 to 2-7).

sections.title: Forensic Investigations
sections.summary: Forensic investigations identify causes of problems that have occurred, e.g., after slope failures or rockfall: locating the sliding surface, groundwater at failure and continuing movement, plus parameters for remedial design, often with urgency.
sections.body: Forensic investigations resemble design investigations in using advanced boring, sampling and testing, but focus on causes of problems that have occurred and so are more directed to specific locations. After slope failures or rockfall they commonly locate the observed sliding surface, characterize groundwater when the slide occurred and determine whether movement continues, often adding measurements for remedial design parameters; they are often done with some emergency and may use non-routine equipment and techniques. (p. 2-7)
key_points: Identify causes of problems that have occurred (p. 2-7).
Slides: sliding surface, groundwater at failure, continuing movement (p. 2-7).

sections.title: Investigations for Design-Build Projects
sections.summary: For design-build, the owner provides enough characterization for bidders to design and price confidently and to limit changed condition claims, more than a routine preliminary investigation but less than final design; the design-builder investigates further after award.
sections.body: Owners of design-build or similar projects should provide characterization sufficient for bidders to develop designs and estimate costs confidently and to reduce changed site condition claims, generally characterizing stratigraphy, soil and rock properties and groundwater. Since facility arrangement and loads are unknown before award, the owner cannot provide everything for final design; the design-build organization conducts additional investigations after award. Owner investigations should be more extensive than routine preliminary investigations (section 2.2.2) but seldom reach final design rigor (section 2.2.3). (p. 2-7)
key_points: Owner data sufficient for confident bids; fewer claims (p. 2-7).
More than preliminary, less than final design investigation (p. 2-7).
Design-builder investigates further after award (p. 2-7).

sections.title: Geotechnical Reporting Documents
sections.summary: Common reporting documents are field investigation logs, geotechnical data reports and geotechnical design reports (and, in special cases, baseline reports); detailed content recommendations are in Chapter 13.
sections.body: Investigations generate several documents, most commonly field investigation logs, geotechnical data reports and geotechnical design reports, described generally in sections 2.3.1 to 2.3.4; detailed descriptions and recommended content are in Chapter 13. (p. 2-8)
sections.applicability: Geotechnical reporting document types and their appropriate use in project contracts

sections.title: Field Investigation Logs
sections.summary: Field investigation logs (boring, test pit, in situ test, groundwater and geophysical) show stratigraphy, material descriptions, groundwater observations and test results, and should note difficult drilling, fluid loss, rod drops and borehole instability.
sections.body: The most common products are field investigation logs: boring logs, test pit logs, in situ test logs (CPT, DMT, VST), groundwater monitoring logs and geophysical survey reports. Form and content vary, but logs generally show stratigraphy, engineering descriptions of soil and rock, groundwater observations and test measurements; they should preferably include field observations such as difficult drilling, loss of drilling fluid, "rod drops" that may indicate karst, and borehole instability that may indicate flowing sands. (p. 2-8)
key_points: Stratigraphy, descriptions, groundwater, test results (p. 2-8).
Note difficult drilling, fluid loss, rod drops, instability (p. 2-8).
sections.applicability: Geotechnical reporting document types and their appropriate use in project contracts

sections.title: Geotechnical Data Reports
sections.summary: Geotechnical data reports present the investigations, logs and test results, brief for preliminary work and lengthy for design investigations; they hold only factual data, so they are often bid documents, essential to design-build, and may become legally binding.
sections.body: A geotechnical data report generally describes the investigations, field logs and laboratory and field test results, its content varying with the investigation: brief for preliminary investigations (index tests), lengthy for design or special investigations (index and "performance" properties); reports may also cover geophysical or specialized investigations and relevant desk study data. All data reports (p. 2-9) include only factual data, without interpretations or recommendations; hence they are sometimes part of plans and bid documents, are essential to design-build contracts, may become legally binding and influence claims, change orders and costs. (pp. 2-8 to 2-9)
key_points: Only factual data, no interpretation (p. 2-9).
Often part of bid documents; may be legally binding (p. 2-9).
sections.applicability: Geotechnical reporting document types and their appropriate use in project contracts

sections.title: Geotechnical Design Reports
sections.summary: Geotechnical design reports add interpretation: site descriptions, stratigraphy, groundwater, hazards, design parameters, analyses and recommendations; they are the complete characterization but are rarely bid documents.
sections.body: Geotechnical design reports include much more than factual data: detailed site descriptions, analysis and design methods and results, their interpretation, and design and construction recommendations, with descriptions of materials, stratigraphy, observed and anticipated groundwater, hazards and risks, and interpretations of design parameters, plus much of the factual data or references to data reports. They can be considered the "complete" characterization and ultimate end product, but because they include subjective interpretations they are rarely, if ever, part of plans and bid documents; they document design assumptions and may have legal ramifications depending on location and law. (p. 2-9)
key_points: Interpretations, analyses and recommendations (p. 2-9).
Complete characterization; rarely bid documents (p. 2-9).
sections.applicability: Geotechnical reporting document types and their appropriate use in project contracts

sections.title: Geotechnical Baseline Reports
sections.summary: A geotechnical baseline report (GBR, ASCE 2007) sets a contractually binding baseline interpretation of ground conditions accepted by all parties before construction, the basis for ground-condition claims and change orders.
sections.body: In special cases such as design-build, products may be used for a "geotechnical baseline report" (GBR) (ASCE, 2007), establishing a contractually binding interpretation of ground conditions. Content resembles the interpretations of design reports (p. 2-10), but a GBR sets a "baseline" accepted by all parties before construction, contractually binding and the basis for claims and change orders on ground conditions (see Chapter 13). (pp. 2-9 to 2-10)
key_points: GBR: contractually binding baseline (ASCE, 2007) (p. 2-9).
Basis for ground-condition claims and change orders (p. 2-10).

sections.title: Benefits of Site Characterization
sections.summary: Characterization pays when benefits exceed costs: more reliable design parameters allow efficient designs; early hazard identification lets risks be avoided cheaply; accurate stratigraphy and groundwater reduce quantity errors, claims, change orders and bid costs (Boeckmann and Loehr, 2016).
sections.body: Benefits arise in planning, design, construction and operation, financial and in safety and mobility; if they exceed investigation costs, the investigations add value. Common sources: (1) more reliable design parameters allow more efficient designs, since design reliability depends on parameter reliability, while less reliable or ambiguous parameters force conservative and costlier designs; (2) early identification of hazards allows relocation or suitable foundation selection, while late identification makes redesign or remediation far costlier; (3) accurate stratigraphy, groundwater and material types affect quantities (excavation, fill, driven piles), and incomplete characterization (p. 2-11) increases claims, change orders and overruns (Boeckmann and Loehr, 2016) and contractor risk and bids. Combined benefits can dramatically affect project and agency budgets (see Chapter 3). (pp. 2-10 to 2-11)
key_points: More reliable parameters, more efficient designs (p. 2-10).
Early hazard identification is cheaper (p. 2-10).
Accurate stratigraphy reduces claims and bids (Boeckmann and Loehr, 2016) (pp. 2-10 to 2-11).
